opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it changed my mind quite a bit. Before I'd spent real time around them, I assumed the uncanny valley would be a big barrier. The intuition is that the closer something gets to looking human without quite getting there, the creepier it feels, and that people just wouldn't want these things in their homes.

When you're actually in a room with a Unitree robot, the reaction is very different from what I expected. People aren't creeped out. They're curious, they laugh, they want to touch it and play with it. I think part of that is that Unitree didn't try to make them look human. They look like robots, a bit mechanical and a bit cute, closer to a pet or a character than a fake person. So you never land in the valley. You stay on the friendly side of it.

The other thing I noticed is that movement matters much more than appearance. When a robot moves fluidly, catches its balance, or does something a bit playful, people project personality onto it almost immediately. It's the same thing we do with dogs or even with a Roomba bumping around. That emotional connection comes surprisingly fast.

So my takeaway is that the uncanny valley is mostly a design problem, not a fundamental limit. If you go for hyper-realistic human faces and skin, you probably will hit it. If you embrace being a robot and make it expressive and approachable, social acceptance may come much faster than people think. Kids especially have no hesitation at all. I think the barriers will be more about price, safety, and usefulness than about people finding them creepy.

r001.rationale: The response says real-world time around Unitree robots changed the speaker’s view, but it attributes reduced creepiness to their robot-like design and movement. It does not suggest that repeated exposure itself diminishes the uncanny valley as a barrier.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it changed my mind quite a bit. I used to think the uncanny valley would be a real barrier, that people would find a human-shaped machine moving around their living room deeply unsettling. And then you actually watch a Unitree G1 or H1 walk into a room, and the reaction is almost the opposite. People laugh, they film it, they want to touch it. There's something about the fact that these robots are clearly robots, with the exposed joints and the matte plastic and the sort of childlike proportions on the smaller ones, that defuses the creepiness entirely.

I think the uncanny valley is really about failed imitation of a human face and skin, that Japanese android aesthetic where it's almost but not quite right. Unitree didn't go there at all. They made something that looks like a very capable toy, and it turns out that's much more socially acceptable than something that looks like a slightly dead person.

The other thing that struck me is price. When a humanoid costs the equivalent of a used car, it stops being a science-fiction object and becomes a gadget. And we're very good at accepting gadgets. We don't ask whether a drone is uncanny, we ask what it can do. I suspect that's where humanoids are heading too. The acceptance question is going to be about usefulness and reliability, not about whether the thing triggers some primal discomfort.

So my current view is that the uncanny valley is a design choice you can simply avoid, and the Chinese manufacturers in particular have figured that out faster than a lot of the Western labs that were chasing realism.

r001.rationale: The response says seeing Unitree robots changed the speaker’s view and describes positive reactions, but it does not suggest that repeated exposure diminishes the uncanny valley.

astra-6.text:
Seeing the Unitree robots made me less convinced that the uncanny valley is going to be a fundamental barrier. They’re clearly machines, but there’s something quite endearing about the way they move. You don’t necessarily need a robot to look like a person to feel comfortable around it.

I think a lot depends on the expectations its appearance creates. If it looks almost human, you expect human behavior, and small differences can feel strange. If it’s obviously a robot, you can accept it on its own terms. So I’m more inclined to see this as a design challenge than a hard limit on social acceptance. Of course, finding a robot charming in a video is different from wanting it moving around your home.

r001.rationale: The candidate says seeing Unitree robots made the uncanny valley seem less like a fundamental barrier, but it does not suggest that repeated exposure is what may diminish the barrier.

sol-6.1.text:
Seeing the Unitree robots made me less convinced that the uncanny valley will be a fundamental barrier. You see them move, and there’s something immediately fascinating about them. They don’t have to look exactly like us for us to respond to them socially.

I think a lot will depend on behavior. Does the robot move predictably? Is it useful? Do you feel comfortable around it? The uncanny valley may matter for some designs, but I’m less sure it will determine whether people accept humanoids overall.
